title: Kurseong and Mirik on a Budget: What Things Cost
meta_description: Indicative 2025–26 prices for Kurseong, Mirik and the tea valleys: shared jeeps, homestays, boats, cars and food, with two day budgets and money-saving tips.
summary: Kurseong, Mirik and the tea valleys cost about ₹1,500–2,000 a person a day on a shoestring and ₹3,000–5,000 at a comfortable level. Shared jeeps at ₹150–200 a seat and village homestays at ₹1,200–1,800 with meals keep costs low. Private cars and peak-week hotels are what push budgets up.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: The middle hills between Siliguri and Darjeeling are the cheapest part of the Darjeeling hills to travel well. Kurseong and Mirik are both under 2.5 hours from Siliguri by shared jeep, so you do not lose a day or a large fare getting up. The villages around them, Sittong, Latpanchar, Chimney and the Makaibari estate, are full of family homestays that charge one price for a bed, dinner and breakfast, and that price is usually lower than a town hotel room plus two restaurant meals.

A careful solo traveller can manage on ₹1,500–2,000 a day. A couple sharing a modest hotel room and hiring a car for one day of sightseeing will spend about ₹3,000–5,000 each per day. The numbers below are indicative for 2025–26, for budget and mid-range travel. Fares, fees and toy train tickets change, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Two day budgets that work
paras: A shoestring day assumes a homestay bed with dinner and breakfast, a light lunch of momos or noodles, tea from stalls, one short jeep ride and walks instead of paid sightseeing. A value day assumes half a double room in a clean hotel with hot water, sit-down meals, a share of a car for half a day and a boat on the lake or a tea tasting.

Add the journey up and down separately. A shared jeep each way adds ₹300–400 to the whole trip. A reserved car shared by four people costs roughly ₹500–750 each per direction, which is why families with luggage often find it worth paying.

sections.heading: Getting around for less
paras: Shared jeeps are the backbone of travel here. They leave Siliguri from the Hill Cart Road stands near Siliguri Junction and the Tenzing Norgay bus terminus when every seat is full, from early morning until mid-afternoon. Front seats beside the driver cost the same and are worth asking for if you get carsick on the bends. Between Kurseong and Darjeeling jeeps run all day; between Mirik and Darjeeling they are fewer after 2 pm.

The villages are where costs rise. Sittong, Latpanchar and Ahaldara have only a few local jeeps, usually leaving the village early and returning in the afternoon, so most visitors hire a car. You can cut this cost in two ways: share the car with another family from your homestay, or take a jeep to Kurseong and ask your host to collect you there, which is shorter than coming from Siliguri. Within Kurseong itself, Dow Hill, Eagle's Crag, the station and the bazaar are all walkable, and Makaibari is a 45-minute walk down the Pankhabari road.

Two smaller savings add up over a week. Buy jeep seats at the stand rather than through a hotel, which adds a commission, and travel in the morning, when jeeps fill fastest and you are not left paying for empty seats at 4 pm. If a jeep is short of passengers late in the day, the driver may ask the group to split the fare of the missing seats; agree the amount before you set off.

sections.heading: What a homestay price includes
paras: Homestays are the best value in this land, but the word covers a wide range. In Sittong, Latpanchar and Chimney it usually means a room or two in a family house, sometimes a separate cottage built for guests, with a shared or attached bathroom. The ₹1,200–1,800 per person normally covers the bed, dinner and breakfast. Dinner is rice, dal, a vegetable or two, a pickle and often chicken or eggs; breakfast is puri or paratha with potato curry, or bread and eggs, with tea.

Ask before you book about what is extra. Lunch is often ₹150–250 if you want it at the house. A packed breakfast and flask of tea for an Ahaldara sunrise may cost ₹100–200. Bonfires in winter, guided walks and pick-ups from Kurseong or Siliguri are all charged separately. Hot water can be from a geyser, a solar heater or a bucket heated on the stove, which matters in December and January when nights fall to 5 °C at Chimney.

The Makaibari village homestays work a little differently: the programme places guests with tea workers' families on the estate, and the rate, about ₹1,500–2,000 per person with meals, is set through the coordinators rather than by each house. A factory visit or tasting is extra and depends on the season.

sections.heading: Where people overspend
paras: We see the same three mistakes every season. The first is the bundled sightseeing package. In Mirik, drivers offer a 'points' tour covering the lake, Bokar monastery, a viewpoint, a tea garden and an orange orchard, often for ₹1,500–2,500. The lake, the monastery and the bazaar are within walking distance of each other; you only need a car for Tingling, Sourenee or Gopaldhara, and those are easiest seen on the way in or out.

The second is the lone-passenger reserved car on a road where shared jeeps run every half hour. The third is arriving without a booking on a festival weekend, when lakeside hotels in Mirik and the few rooms near Kurseong station can double in price. Book ahead for October and late May, or come in November and March, when rooms are easier and cheaper.
list: Walk Mirik lake's 3.5 km road instead of paying for a pony or a car
Buy tea in the estate shop or Kurseong bazaar, not at airport counters
Eat your homestay's dinner; it is included and usually the best meal of the day
Carry cash: village homestays and jeep stands rarely take cards, and ATMs are only in the towns

sections.heading: Sample trip costs
paras: Three nights from Siliguri on a shoestring, one in Kurseong and two in a Makaibari or Sittong homestay, comes to about ₹6,000–7,500 per person including jeeps, a shared car to Sittong and simple lunches. Four nights at a value level, two in Kurseong and two in Mirik, with a car between the towns and for one day of sightseeing, runs about ₹12,000–16,000 per person for a couple. Our own planned journeys in this land start at about ₹5,500 per person for two nights.

International backpackers pay the same jeep fares and homestay rates as Indian travellers here; there are no permits and no foreigner surcharges for the lake or the monasteries. Students travelling in a group of four or five can bring the daily cost close to ₹1,300 each by sharing one homestay room and one car for the village days.
Whatever you plan, keep ₹1,000–2,000 spare for the day a landslide closes a road and you need a longer route or an extra night. That happens most often between late June and September.

faqs.q: How much does a trip to Kurseong and Mirik cost per day?
faqs.a: On a shoestring, about ₹1,500–2,000 per person per day, using shared jeeps and a homestay that includes dinner and breakfast. At a comfortable value level, with half a hotel double, restaurant meals and a share of a car, expect ₹3,000–5,000. Festival weeks and the May–June holidays raise room prices, so book early or travel in November or March for the best rates.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to get from Siliguri to Kurseong?
faqs.a: A shared jeep from the Hill Cart Road stands near Siliguri Junction or the Tenzing Norgay bus terminus, at about ₹150–200 a seat. Jeeps leave when full from early morning, roughly every 30–45 minutes, and take 1.5 hours by the Rohini road or up to 2.5 hours by the old Hill Cart Road. The toy train is slower and, when it runs, often costs more.

faqs.q: How much do homestays cost in Sittong and Latpanchar?
faqs.a: Most family homestays in Sittong and Latpanchar charge about ₹1,200–1,800 per person per night including dinner and breakfast. Rooms are simple, often with attached bathrooms and hot water by geyser or bucket. Prices rise a little in orange season and on long weekends. Lunch, packed breakfasts for sunrise trips and car hire are usually extra, so agree on them when you book.

Usually, yes. Budget hotel doubles in Mirik's Krishnanagar start at about ₹1,200, a little below Darjeeling, and food prices are similar or lower. The jeep from Siliguri costs ₹150–200 against ₹250–350 for Darjeeling. Mirik has fewer paid sights too, since the lake walk and Bokar monastery are free. Peak weekends during Durga Puja are the exception.

faqs.q: Do I need a car for sightseeing in Kurseong?
faqs.a: Not for the town itself. The station, bazaar, Eagle's Crag, Dow Hill and Makaibari are all walkable, though Dow Hill is a 1–1.5 hour climb. A half-day car at ₹1,500–2,200 makes sense if you want Giddapahar, Dow Hill, Chimney and a tea estate in one morning, or if you have older family members who should avoid the steep lanes.

faqs.q: How much does boating cost on Mirik lake?
faqs.a: A rowing boat on Sumendu Lake costs about ₹150–300 for roughly 20 minutes, depending on the boat and season. Pony rides along the lake road are also offered, priced by distance. Both are optional: walking the 3.5 km road around the lake and crossing the footbridge costs nothing and takes about an hour at an easy pace. Rates are indicative; check at the boat stand.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs in Kurseong, Mirik and the villages?
faqs.a: Kurseong and Mirik both have bank ATMs in the main bazaar areas, though they can run dry on holiday weekends. Sittong, Latpanchar, Chimney and the tea estate villages have none. Carry enough cash for homestays, cars and food before you leave town. UPI works in many shops and some homestays, but mobile signal in the valleys can be weak.

faqs.q: How much does Darjeeling tea cost at the estates?
faqs.a: Expect about ₹300–1,500 for 100 g of estate tea, depending on the flush, grade and garden. First flush and special hand-made lots sit at the top of that range. Kurseong bazaar and Mirik shops sell packets from Makaibari, Castleton, Gopaldhara and other gardens. Avoid cheap loose tea sold as Darjeeling at stalls with no garden name.

faqs.q: How can families save money on a Kurseong and Mirik trip?
faqs.a: Share one reserved car for the whole family when you have luggage or older travellers, and use shared jeeps for short hops where they run often. Choose homestays that include meals, walk around Mirik lake rather than taking ponies, buy tea in the bazaar, and travel in November or March, when room prices are lower than in May or Puja weeks.
